latin: Age! Properemus<sup>1</sup> ad stationem<sup>2</sup>! Tramen post viginti minutas abiturum<sup>3</sup> est.
Ad stationem properamus. Ubi est tesseraria?
Da, quaeso, tres tesseras secundae classis<sup>4</sup> Forum Julii<sup>5</sup>, aditus et reditus.

Ecce, domne! Quindecim nummis<sup>6</sup> et sexaginta centesimis. Nolite<sup>7</sup> properare! Tramen vestrum dimidiae horae moram habebit neque<sup>8</sup> ante meridiem<sup>9</sup> abibit<sup>10</sup>.
Festinatio sitim excitavit. Otium est poculi bibendi<sup>11</sup>. In stationis thermopolium eamus!
Heus, puer! — Quid bibere vis? — Nolo bibere; malo aliquid comedere. Habesne pastilla farcta<sup>12</sup>?
Puer. — Habeo, domne. Paucas minutas exspectandum<sup>13</sup> est. Ecce plaustrum bajulusque qui glaciem<sup>14</sup> mihi affert.
Bajulus. — En tibi quinque partes glaciei quas cottidie afferre soleo.
Puer. — Mihi ignosce! Quattuor tantum adsunt.
Bajulus. — Hoc mirum est. Certus sum quinque adfuisse. Miror ubi quinta evanuerit...
Subito sibilum locomotricis<sup>15</sup> audimus. Relinquere debemus puerum et bajulum quintam partem glaciei quaerentes<sup>16</sup>.
english: Come on! Let’s hurry to the station! The train is due-to-leave in twenty minutes.
We are hurrying to the station. Where is the ticket seller [fem.]?
Give [me/us], please, three second-class tickets to Fréjus, [return] (of going and of returning).
Here, sir! 15.60 (15 pieces and 60 cents). Don’t [pl.] hurry! Your train will have a half-hour delay and [will] not [leave] before noon (will-go-away).
Haste has [made me thirsty] (stirred up thirst). [There is time to drink a glass] (Leisure there-is of a glass due-to-be-drunk). Let us go into the station(‘s) canteen!
Hey there, [waiter] (boy)! — What [would you like] (do you want) to drink? — I don’t want to drink; [I’d rather] (I prefer to) eat something. Do you have sandwiches?
Waiter. — I do (have), sir. [You will need to wait] a few minutes (to-be-awaited is). Here is the truck and the [deliveryman] (porter) who brings me ice.
Deliveryman. — Here [I have] for you five [blocks] (parts) of ice [as usual] (that every day I am accustomed to bring).
Waiter. — Forgive (to) me! There are only four here.
Deliveryman. — This is strange. I’m sure there were five. I wonder where the fifth one disappeared (perfect subj.).
Suddenly we hear the whistle of the locomotive. We must leave behind the waiter and the deliveryman searching for the fifth block of ice.

footnotes: Properemus (from propero, -as, -are, -avi, -atum) is a subjunctive (with imperative meaning). You will find this same verb again in the present indicative in phrase 2.
Statio, -onis, f., comes from sto, -as, -are, steti, statum, to stand still.
Abiturus, -a, -um, future participle of abeo, -is, -ire, -ii, -itum, to leave.
Classis, -is, f., class (school or category) or fleet (of ships).
Forum, -i, n., public square, market. Julii, gen. of Julius, the emperor who gave his name to the town of Fréjus.
Nummus, -i, m. piece of coinage, usual unit of currency (here, for the franc). Centesimus, -a, -um, hundredth (or cent).
Abibit, future of abire (see above, N. 3).

Bibendus, -a, -um, gerundive of bibo, -is, -ere, bibi, bibitum. You may know the verse by the poet Horace: Nunc est bibendum! Now we must drink! This is, it seems, the origin of the use of Bibendum as the name of the Michelin man!
Fartus, -a, -um, past passive participle of farcio, -is, -ire, farsi, fartum, to fill up, to stuff. Here in the neuter plural: the singular is then pastillum fartum. Pastillum, -i, n., roll.
Exspectandus, -a, -um, gerundive of exspecto, -as, -are, -avi, -atum. Here exspectandum is neuter, because this is an impersonal form.
Locomotrix, -icis, f., word of recent coinage (Vita Latina, No. 19, p. 56), whose feminine gender is perhaps open to argument.
Quaerens, -entis, present (active) participle of quaero, -is, -ere, quaesivi, quaesitum.
comments: In this lesson, only two words are of recent coinage, tramen and locomotrix. Even though they are used by some very serious modern authors, they may not be accepted by certain purists: Concours Général candidates, take heed! All the other words are of good Latin pedigree, which there is no reason not to use in a modern context. Thus the word statio has been used in all periods for a stopping place (see N. 2). A Roman soldier hearing this word thought of a sentry post; but as the subject of conversation is the train, statio can only mean a railway station. Likewise Tessera, -ae, f., was a token for voting or admittance to a theatre. If the word were taken in isolation from the text of today’s lesson, it would be necessary to further specify: tessera viatoria (related to travel) to avoid any confusion. Minuta is the feminine of the past passive participle of minuo, -is, -ere, -ui, -utum, to lessen, which has given us not only minute, but above all menu. Finally vaporarium, -i, n., is the boiler and vaporarius, -a, -um, the corresponding adjective. Of course, the same thing happens in all languages. Thus today the word brake makes us think of the brake of a bicycle or a car; but our ancestors would have thought of the bit in a horse’s mouth: the objects differ, but the function remains the same.

latin: Quid edere vis? — Pastillum farctum edere volo.
Ego bibere malo. Poculum cerevisiae, quaeso!
Qui est hic sibilus? — Nemo sibilat.
Quo intrat hoc tramen sibilans? — In stationem intrat.
Ubi est tramen? — In statione est.
Qua transit? — Per stationem transit?
Unde exit? — E statione exit.
Dicit se locomotricem sibilantem audire. Dicunt se tramen sibilans audisse.
Locomotrices vaporariae atrae sunt; electricae autem clarioris coloris.
english: What do you want to eat? — I want to eat a sandwich.
*I* prefer to drink. A glass of beer, please!
What whistling is this? — Nobody is whistling.
Where (whither) does this train enter whistling? — It enters into the station.
Where is the train? — It is in the station.
Where does it pass through? — It passes through the station.
Where does it leave from? — It leaves from the station.
He says that he hears the locomotive whistling. They say they heard to train whistling.
Steam locomotives are black; electric [ones], on the other hand, are of a brighter color.
